title: Private Prediction via Shrinkage
topic: Social Aspects->Privacy-preserving Statistics and Machine Learning
claim: Upon a hard query, the hypothesis set splits in two, and a random guess restricts it to one half.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, block arrow between them, math labels on regions
description: Two black-and-white panels joined by a bold right-pointing arrow. Each panel has a diagonal line labeled x at its top end, standing for a hard query that splits the hypothesis set. The label C|h(x)=-1 sits at the upper left and C|h(x)=1 at the lower right of the line. The left panel shows seven black dots scattered on both sides of the line, representing the full hypothesis set before the split. The right panel shows six dots, all on the lower-right side (the h(x)=1 side), with none on the h(x)=-1 side. The picture shows the set shrinking to the guessed subspace. There is no color. The eye goes first to the arrow and the diagonal lines, then to the dot clusters.
caption: In the left figure, we illustrate that when a “hard” query x occurs, the current hypothesis set splits into two subspaces, C|h(x)=1 and C|h(x)=−1. We then guess a label uniformly at random (say, 1) and update the hypothesis set by restricting to C|h(x)=1, as shown in the right figure.
abstract: We study differentially private prediction introduced by Dwork and Feldman (COLT 2018): an algorithm receives one labeled sample set $S$ and then answers a stream of unlabeled queries while the output transcript remains $(\varepsilon,Î´)$-differentially private with respect to $S$. Standard composition yields a $\sqrt{T}$ dependence for $T$ queries. We show that this dependence can be reduced to polylogarithmic in $T$ in streaming settings. For an oblivious online adversary and any concept class $\mathcal{C}$, we give a private predictor that answers $T$ queries with $|S|= \tilde{O}(VC(\mathcal{C})^{3.5}\log^{3.5}T)$ labeled examples. For an adaptive online adversary and halfspaces over $\mathbb{R}^d$, we obtain $|S|=\tilde{O}\left(d^{5.5}\log T\right)$.
